quests.hint: Listen carefully for the time expression.
quests.explanation: 'Half past six' means 6:30; 'quarter past six' means 6:15. These clock expressions are very common in British English. Practise saying them clearly - they are essential for making and keeping appointments.
quests.textToSpeak: She usually wakes up at half past six in the morning.
quests.correctAnswer: She usually wakes up at quarter past six in the morning.

quests.hint: Focus on whether the shower is before or after breakfast.
quests.explanation: 'Before' and 'after' are opposite prepositions of time. 'He showers before breakfast' versus 'after breakfast' completely reverses the order of events. Prepositions of time are critical for describing daily routines accurately.
quests.textToSpeak: He always takes a shower before he eats breakfast.
quests.correctAnswer: He always takes a shower after he eats breakfast.

quests.hint: Notice the verb describing how they move to the park.
quests.explanation: 'Walk' and 'jog' describe different speeds of movement on foot. 'Walk' is a normal pace; 'jog' is a slow run, typically for exercise. Both are common verbs in English sentences about exercise routines.
quests.textToSpeak: They walk to the park for exercise every evening.
quests.correctAnswer: They jog to the park for exercise every evening.

quests.hint: Pay attention to the price of the jacket.
quests.explanation: 'Fifty' (50) and 'fifteen' (15) are easily confused in spoken English - 'fifty' stresses the first syllable (FIF-ty), while 'fifteen' stresses the second (fif-TEEN). This is a very common listening challenge.
quests.textToSpeak: The jacket was on sale for fifty pounds.
quests.correctAnswer: The jacket was on sale for fifteen pounds.

quests.hint: Listen for when she went shopping - morning or afternoon.
quests.explanation: 'Morning' and 'afternoon' are the two halves of the daytime. 'The whole morning' and 'the whole afternoon' both suggest a long time spent on an activity - the time-of-day word changes the picture entirely.
quests.textToSpeak: She spent the whole morning looking for a gift.
quests.correctAnswer: She spent the whole afternoon looking for a gift.

quests.hint: Focus on whether he exchanged or returned the shirt.
quests.explanation: To 'exchange' means to swap one item for another; to 'return' means to give it back for a refund. Both are common shopping actions in English. 'I'd like to exchange/return this' are useful phrases for shops.
quests.textToSpeak: He decided to exchange the shirt for a larger size.
quests.correctAnswer: He decided to return the shirt for a larger size.

quests.hint: Listen for which school subject the test was in.
quests.explanation: 'Biology' studies living organisms; 'chemistry' studies substances and reactions. Both are sciences, but they are distinct subjects. School subject names are essential vocabulary for discussing education.
quests.textToSpeak: The students had a biology test on Monday.
quests.correctAnswer: The students had a chemistry test on Monday.

quests.hint: Notice whether she missed the first or last class.
quests.explanation: 'First' and 'last' are opposite ordinal adjectives. 'Missing the first class' means arriving late; 'missing the last class' means leaving early. Small words like these carry big differences in meaning.
quests.textToSpeak: She missed the first class because she was late.
quests.correctAnswer: She missed the last class because she was late.

quests.hint: Pay attention to whether the library opens or closes at nine.
quests.explanation: 'Opens' and 'closes' are antonyms crucial for everyday life. 'The library closes at nine' means you must finish by nine; 'opens at nine' means you cannot enter before nine. A single verb changes the entire meaning.
quests.textToSpeak: The library closes at nine o'clock on weekdays.
quests.correctAnswer: The library opens at nine o'clock on weekdays.

quests.hint: Listen for the type of sandwich she ordered.
quests.explanation: 'Chicken sandwich' and 'tuna sandwich' both follow the pattern '[filling] + sandwich'. In English restaurants, you specify the filling first. Menu vocabulary like this is essential for ordering food confidently.
quests.textToSpeak: She ordered a chicken sandwich and a salad.
quests.correctAnswer: She ordered a tuna sandwich and a salad.

quests.hint: Notice whether the waiter brought the wrong starter or dessert.
quests.explanation: 'Starter' (or 'appetiser') is the first course; 'dessert' is the final, sweet course. In British restaurant English, a meal typically has starter, main course, and dessert - in that order.
quests.textToSpeak: The waiter brought us the wrong dessert.
quests.correctAnswer: The waiter brought us the wrong starter.

quests.hint: Focus on which nationality of food he loves cooking.
quests.explanation: 'Italian food' and 'Thai food' are both popular cuisines. In English, nationality adjectives describe the origin of food: 'Italian pasta', 'Thai curry'. Learning food adjectives helps you discuss restaurants and cooking.
quests.textToSpeak: He loves cooking Italian food at the weekend.
quests.correctAnswer: He loves cooking Thai food at the weekend.

quests.hint: Listen carefully for which days she works from home.
quests.explanation: 'Tuesdays and Thursdays' and 'Mondays and Fridays' are different pairs of weekdays. In modern workplaces, which days you work from home is important information. Listen carefully for day names - they sound quite different.
quests.textToSpeak: She works from home on Tuesdays and Thursdays.
quests.correctAnswer: She works from home on Mondays and Fridays.

quests.hint: Pay attention to how long the presentation lasted.
quests.explanation: 'Forty minutes' and 'twenty minutes' are very different durations. When describing events, the duration (how long something lasts) is often the most important detail - and numbers are easy to mishear.
quests.textToSpeak: The presentation lasted for about forty minutes.
quests.correctAnswer: The presentation lasted for about twenty minutes.

quests.hint: Notice how the report was sent - email or post.
quests.explanation: 'By email' means electronically; 'by post' means physically through the mail service. Both are common ways to send documents. 'Send something by email/post' is standard professional English.
quests.textToSpeak: He sent the report to his manager by email.
quests.correctAnswer: He sent the report to his manager by post.

quests.hint: Listen for which exercise she does.
quests.explanation: 'Swimming' and 'running' are both popular forms of exercise. 'Go swimming' and 'go running' use 'go + verb-ing' - this is the standard English structure for many sports and exercise activities.
quests.textToSpeak: She goes swimming three times a week.
quests.correctAnswer: She goes running three times a week.

quests.hint: Focus on what the doctor recommended more of.
quests.explanation: 'Rest' means relaxing and recovering; 'exercise' means physical activity. Both are health recommendations. 'The doctor recommended more...' is a useful structure for reporting advice in English.
quests.textToSpeak: The doctor recommended more rest and less stress.
quests.correctAnswer: The doctor recommended more exercise and less stress.

quests.hint: Notice what healthy change he made - food or portion size.
quests.explanation: 'Eating healthier food' means choosing nutritious options; 'eating smaller portions' means reducing quantity. Both are weight-management strategies. These are common health topics in everyday English conversations.
quests.textToSpeak: He started eating healthier food last month.
quests.correctAnswer: He started eating smaller portions last month.

quests.hint: Listen for which device she bought for university.
quests.explanation: A 'laptop' is a portable computer with a keyboard; a 'tablet' is a touchscreen device without a physical keyboard. Both are common study tools. Device vocabulary is essential in modern English conversation.
quests.textToSpeak: She bought a new laptop for university.
quests.correctAnswer: She bought a new tablet for university.

quests.hint: Pay attention to whether the internet is slow or fast.
quests.explanation: 'Slow' and 'fast' are opposite adjectives that completely change the meaning when describing internet connections. 'The internet connection is slow/fast' is one of the most common tech complaints or compliments in English.
quests.textToSpeak: The internet connection is very slow today.
quests.correctAnswer: The internet connection is very fast today.

quests.hint: Focus on what he charges before going to bed.
quests.explanation: 'Phone' and 'laptop' are both devices that need charging. In English, 'charge your phone/laptop/watch' is a very frequent phrase in modern daily conversation. The device charged changes the sentence's context entirely.
quests.textToSpeak: He always charges his phone before going to bed.
quests.correctAnswer: He always charges his laptop before going to bed.

quests.hint: Listen for how long the flight takes.
quests.explanation: 'Seven hours' and 'nine hours' are both long-haul flight durations. Flight times are important practical information. 'The flight takes [time]' is a standard phrase in travel conversations.
quests.textToSpeak: The flight to New York takes about seven hours.
quests.correctAnswer: The flight to New York takes about nine hours.

quests.hint: Notice whether she checked in or collected her luggage.
quests.explanation: 'Check in luggage' means to hand it to the airline before the flight; 'collect luggage' means to pick it up from the baggage carousel after landing. These are opposite actions at opposite ends of a journey.
quests.textToSpeak: She checked in her luggage at the airport.
quests.correctAnswer: She collected her luggage at the airport.

quests.hint: Pay attention to how long the train was delayed.
quests.explanation: 'Thirty minutes' and 'twenty minutes' are different delay lengths. In everyday English, expressing how long you were delayed is very common. 'The train was delayed by...' is a useful passive construction.
quests.textToSpeak: The train was delayed by thirty minutes this morning.
quests.correctAnswer: The train was delayed by twenty minutes this morning.

quests.hint: Listen for what time the film starts.
quests.explanation: 'Eight o'clock' and 'six o'clock' are two hours apart but can sound similar in fast speech. 'The film starts at...' is a very common phrase for discussing cinema plans - always listen carefully for the time.
quests.textToSpeak: The film starts at eight o'clock this evening.
quests.correctAnswer: The film starts at six o'clock this evening.

quests.hint: Notice whether she listened to or watched the news.
quests.explanation: You 'listen to' the radio but 'watch' television - the verb changes with the medium. This is an important English collocation. 'Listen to + radio/podcast/music' and 'watch + TV/film/video' are fixed patterns.
quests.textToSpeak: She listened to the news on the radio.
quests.correctAnswer: She watched the news on television.

quests.hint: Focus on what he read - a book or an article.
quests.explanation: A 'book' is a long, bound publication; an 'article' is a shorter piece of writing in a magazine or online. 'Read a book' and 'read an article' are both very common English phrases for describing leisure reading.
quests.textToSpeak: He read a very interesting book last weekend.
quests.correctAnswer: He read a very interesting article last weekend.

quests.hint: Listen for how many years her parents have been married.
quests.explanation: 'Thirty years' and 'twenty years' are a decade apart - a significant difference when describing marriage. The present perfect 'have been married for...' is the correct structure for ongoing states from the past to the present.
quests.textToSpeak: Her parents have been married for thirty years.
quests.correctAnswer: Her parents have been married for twenty years.

quests.hint: Pay attention to what the grandmother bakes best.
quests.explanation: 'Apple pie' and 'lemon cake' are both homemade baked goods. Describing food specialities is a lovely conversational topic. 'My grandmother makes the best...' is a natural, affectionate phrase in English.
quests.textToSpeak: My grandmother makes the best apple pie.
quests.correctAnswer: My grandmother makes the best lemon cake.

quests.hint: Notice whether his brother is older or younger.
quests.explanation: 'Younger brother' and 'older brother' are opposites for sibling age. In English, 'older' and 'younger' (not 'elder' and 'junior' in casual speech) are the standard words for comparing ages within families.
quests.textToSpeak: His younger brother is studying at university.
quests.correctAnswer: His older brother is studying at university.
